title: Is the Resurrection Real and Relevant? Evidence and Hope
metaDescription: Can we actually trust that Jesus rose from the dead? A look at 1 Corinthians 15 on the evidence for the resurrection and why it changes everything for your life.
bodyHtml:
Every day we answer small questions: which shirt, which restaurant. We also answer bigger ones: where to live, who to marry. But underneath all of those sit the deepest questions of all — the ones that reach the root of why we exist. This Easter, our new series "Hard Questions, Real Answers" begins with the biggest question of them all: did Jesus really rise from the dead, and if He did, does it actually matter for your life?

Here is why this question is not just interesting but urgent: if Jesus really walked out of the grave, then your whole life belongs at His feet, with Him as Savior and Lord at the center. But if He did not, we are all wasting a beautiful Sunday morning. There is no comfortable middle ground. So let's look honestly at the evidence and the implications, walking through the Apostle Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 15.

Believing the Resurrection Is Reasonable

Faith in the resurrection is not blind belief. Paul roots his claim in eyewitnesses:

"For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, and then to the Twelve. After that, he appeared to more than five hundred of the brothers and sisters at the same time, most of whom are still living... Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles, and last of all he appeared to me also, as to one abnormally born." (1 Corinthians 15:3–8)

Notice what Paul is doing. He is not simply asserting a private belief; he is pointing to people you could go and interview. Most of those five hundred witnesses were still alive. In effect he says, "Don't take my word for it — go ask them." That is the language of evidence, not legend.

Most historians, including skeptical ones, agree on a few things: Jesus lived, Jesus was crucified, and His tomb was found empty. If you reject the resurrection, you still owe an explanation for that empty tomb. Consider the common alternatives:

  • The swoon theory — that Jesus merely fainted. Yet the Romans knew how to kill, and Jesus was brutally whipped and beaten before He was crucified. Even if He had somehow survived, a badly injured man could not have rolled away a heavy stone, and anyone who saw Him would have seen a dying man, not a risen Lord.
  • The legend theory — that the resurrection developed over centuries. But the creed Paul passes on in 1 Corinthians 15 goes back to the church's earliest days, and the Gospels were written within 20 to 40 years of Jesus' life. Legends do not form that quickly while eyewitnesses can still object.
  • The hallucination theory — that grieving followers imagined it. But five hundred people do not share the same hallucination.
  • The conspiracy theory — that the disciples stole the body. Yet these ordinary men went on to suffer and die rather than recant. People may die for something false they believe is true; they do not knowingly die for what they know is a lie.

Even a detail like the first witnesses being women — whose testimony carried little legal weight in that culture — argues for authenticity. No one inventing a story would include it. It's there because it happened.

The Resurrection Can Reach Anyone

Paul does not just argue for the resurrection; he is living proof of its power.

"For I am the least of the apostles and do not even deserve to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace to me was not without effect." (1 Corinthians 15:9–10)

Before he was a church planter, Paul was a church persecutor — approving executions, hunting believers. Any of us would have written him off. Yet God chose him and transformed him. That's the point: the resurrection can reach anyone. It does not matter how long or how far you have been running from God. Grace is not based on what you deserve; it is based on who God is. And grace, when truly received, is always transformational. Jesus made the same point when He said of a forgiven woman, "her many sins have been forgiven — as her great love has shown" (Luke 7:47). The more we grasp how much we've been loved, the more naturally we live for Him.

The Resurrection Gives Living Hope

Finally, Paul explains why all of this matters for the future:

"And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins... If only for this life we have hope in Christ, we are of all people most to be pitied. But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep." (1 Corinthians 15:17–20)

Because Jesus rose, those who trust Him will rise too. Peter calls it "a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, and into an inheritance that can never perish, spoil or fade" (1 Peter 1:3–4). Biblical hope is not wishful thinking about the weather; it is confident expectation of a secure future. And because that hope is a gift you never earned, it can never be taken from you — which means no fear in life and no fear in death. Death becomes not a dead end but a doorway.

A Takeaway to Sit With

Jesus told doubting Thomas, "Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed" (John 20:29). You may not have it all figured out, and that's okay — it is not the strength of your faith that saves you but the depth of His love. So the honest question this Easter is simple: is the resurrection real and relevant to you? Not, have you attended church or memorized verses — but have you actually entrusted your life to the risen Jesus?

If that question is stirring something in you, we would love to walk with you. Whether you are a longtime believer or exploring faith for the first time here in Livermore and the Tri-Valley, there is a place for you at Arroyo Church.
